# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book began as a question about a street sign.

Stanford's campus and the towns around it are named after the people in this
story. Serra. Hoover. Terman. Page Mill. Sand Hill. Addison. The names are not
decoration and they are not accidents. They are a record of who held power in
California and in what order, laid down in the one medium that outlasts
newspapers, lawsuits, and reputations: the street grid.

Read the grid carefully enough and it tells you the argument of this book.

*Cardinal* is a history of how California became the most powerful economic
force in the modern world. The standard version of that history involves
garages, dropouts, and genius. That version is not false. It is incomplete in a
specific way: it describes the people who arrived at the chokepoints without
describing how the chokepoints got there, who paid to build them, and why they
keep appearing in the same forty-mile corridor generation after generation.

The book covers roughly two hundred and fifty years, from a Spanish expedition
logging baptisms in Alta California in 1769 to an inauguration platform in
Washington in 2025 where the founders of technology companies stood closer to
the president than most of his cabinet. It argues that the same mechanism
operated throughout, in different institutional costume each time, and that one
institution connects every phase of it.

Nothing in these pages is a secret. Every document cited is public. The
railroad's land grants were printed in the statutes. The university's founding
charter is a matter of record. The defence contracts, the patent filings, the
venture returns, the market shares — all disclosed, all available, most of it
online. This is not a history of concealment.

It is a history of something harder to see than a secret, which is a pattern
running in plain sight for long enough that it stops looking like a pattern and
starts looking like the weather.
